title: JDK 27 and JDK 28: What We Know So Far
gist: JDK 27, the second non-LTS release after JDK 25, has reached its first release candidate with a locked feature set of nine JEPs and a GA date of September 15, 2026; JDK 28 follows in March 2027 with six JEPs already targeted. The substantive shifts are defaults rather than new APIs — G1 becomes the garbage collector in all environments, compact object headers become the default HotSpot layout, and post-quantum hybrid key exchange lands for TLS 1.3 — while Valhalla's Value Objects finally reaches preview in JDK 28.

insights.claim: JDK 27's feature set is frozen at nine JEPs following the fork to the stabilization repository in early June 2026, with only critical regressions admissible via the Fix-Request process, and GA is fixed for September 15, 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The release contents are now decision-grade for anyone planning Java platform upgrades or vendor JDK migrations in Q4 2026.
insights.quote: As per the release schedule, JDK 27 will be formally released on September 15, 2026.
insights.locator: JDK 27, the second non-LTS release since JDK 25

insights.claim: JDK 27's nine features cluster into just four areas — Core Java Library, HotSpot, Security Library and the language specification — with HotSpot changes carrying the most operational weight.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Runtime-behaviour changes, not API additions, are what will require regression testing on upgrade — plan validation effort accordingly.
insights.locator: The final set of nine (9) new features

insights.claim: JEP 523 makes G1 the default garbage collector in all environments rather than only server-class ones, so any JVM run without an explicit collector flag will now select G1.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Small-container and desktop Java workloads that previously fell back to Serial GC will see different latency and footprint characteristics on upgrade without any config change.
insights.quote: default in all environments, rather than just server environments.

insights.claim: JEP 534 promotes Compact Object Headers, delivered in JDK 25, to the default HotSpot object header layout in JDK 27.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Heap footprint reductions arrive by default for heap-heavy JVM fleets — a real cloud-cost lever that requires no application change.
insights.quote: proposes to make JEP 519, Compact Object Headers, delivered in JDK 25, the default object header layout in the HotSpot JVM

insights.claim: JEP 536 adds in-process redaction to JDK Flight Recorder so sensitive command-line arguments, environment variables and system properties are scrubbed before the recording completes.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Removes a standing compliance objection to shipping JFR recordings off-host, which should broaden production profiling adoption in regulated environments.
insights.quote: proposes to enhance the JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) to redact sensitive information before the JFR completes its recording

insights.claim: JDK 27 ships post-quantum hybrid key exchange for TLS 1.3 as a finished Security Library feature (JEP 527), not a preview.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Post-quantum readiness reaches the mainstream enterprise runtime — a milestone for harvest-now-decrypt-later remediation timelines in Java estates.
insights.quote: JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3
insights.locator: Two (2) of these new features are categorized under Security Library

themes.theme: Long-Running Previews and the Valhalla Dependency

insights.claim: The Vector API enters its twelfth incubation with no substantial implementation changes since JDK 25, and is explicitly blocked from promotion until Project Valhalla features become available as previews.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Java's SIMD story remains gated on Valhalla — a structural reason Java lags for numeric and ML-adjacent workloads regardless of JIT improvements.
insights.quote: The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features.

insights.claim: Structured Concurrency reaches a seventh preview in JDK 27 after six previews and two incubations dating back to JDK 19, indicating a long stabilization tail for Project Loom's concurrency model.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Teams betting architecture on structured concurrency should still assume API churn; the finalization date remains unannounced.
insights.quote: treat groups of related tasks running in different threads as a single unit of work, thereby streamlining error handling and cancellation, improving reliability, and enhancing observability.

insights.claim: Primitive Types in Patterns reaches a fifth preview with tightened dominance checks in switch and a refined definition of unconditional exactness, showing Amber is still adjusting semantics rather than polishing syntax.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Semantic changes this late in preview mean early adopters of primitive patterns face recompilation risk on each JDK bump.
insights.quote: Changes include: enhance the definition of unconditional exactness; and the application of tighter dominance checks in switch constructs.

themes.theme: JDK 28: Valhalla Preview, JSON in the Platform, Port Deprecation

insights.claim: JEP 401, Value Objects, is targeted for preview in JDK 28, defining objects that contain only final fields, have no identity, and are distinguished solely by their field values.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The gating dependency for Vector API promotion and for Java's memory-layout competitiveness finally enters preview — the milestone to watch for the whole Valhalla thesis.
insights.quote: this JEP proposes to enhance the language with value objects, defined as objects that: only contain final fields; do not have identity; and are solely distinguished by the values of their respective fields

insights.claim: JEP 540 brings a Simple JSON API into the JDK as an incubator, implementing RFC 8259 and superseding the withdrawn JEP 198 Light-Weight JSON API, removing the need for an external library for basic parsing and generation.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A platform-level JSON API pressures the long tail of third-party JSON libraries in the Java ecosystem for simple use cases.
insights.quote: This JEP defines a simple, standard API for parsing and generating JSON documents without the need for an external library.

insights.claim: JEP 541 deprecates the macOS/x64 port for removal because Apple no longer supports that architecture, following the same maintenance-cost logic as the earlier Windows 32-bit x86 deprecation.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Intel Mac Java build and CI targets have a visible end-of-life; toolchain and vendor-support planning should account for it now.
insights.quote: This JEP proposes to deprecate the macOS/x64 port as Apple no longer supports this architecture.

insights.claim: JEP 535 makes Shenandoah's generational mode the default in JDK 28 and deprecates the non-generational mode for future removal, while a draft JEP targets faster ZGC startup by allocating a small initial heap.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Both alternative collectors are converging on generational designs and startup efficiency — relevant to serverless and short-lived JVM cost profiles.
insights.quote: Startup time can be minimized by creating only a small initial heap that reduces the overhead of the operating system.

insights.claim: PEM Encodings of Cryptographic Objects is proposed to finalize in JDK 28 as JEP 542 after three preview rounds, with the DEREncodable interface renamed to BinaryEncodable and the PEM record class reclassified as a regular class.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Code written against the preview API will need a rename; a small but concrete migration item for cryptography-heavy Java codebases.
insights.quote: a rename of the DEREncodable interface to BinaryEncodable to more accurately describe the binary data stored in PEM text
